extracted.intended_audience: self-directed beginners aiming for Japanese fluency (zero-knowledge to intermediate)
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step self-study road map for learners starting with zero Japanese and aiming for fluent reading, writing (typing), listening, and speaking. Emphasizes an early focus on kanji/vocabulary, SRS, and deliberate progression through measurable milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to Read Hiragana
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to read all hiragana (including contractions) without cheating before moving on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1 day to 1 week. Use mnemonics and worksheets to learn reading quickly; focus on reading (not handwriting) initially because typing covers 99% of modern writing. Read the 'Japanese Pronunciation, Part 1' section before starting hiragana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic Japanese Pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire correct pronunciation of hiragana and key Japanese sounds, including pitch accent awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'Japanese Sounds and Your Mouth' and 'Important Differences.' Ensure you can pronounce all hiragana correctly before proceeding. Mimic vocabulary audio and be conscious of pitch accent even if mastering it is difficult early on (gives a leg up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to Type Hiragana
rubrics_metrics.description: Install a Japanese IME and learn to type hiragana, including contractions, small tsu, and dakuten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1–2 days (or less). Follow a 'How to Type in Japanese' guide and only focus on hiragana until comfortable; once confident, move on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Concept of Kanji (Start Early)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin kanji study as soon as you can read and type hiragana—do not postpone kanji until later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: kanji leads to vocabulary which aids grammar; postponing kanji makes textbook study slow and frustrating. Read 'On’yomi vs. Kun’yomi' to understand readings before learning actual kanji.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning Kanji & Stockpiling Kanji Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn kanji meanings and readings prioritized by real usage (the most important meanings/readings used 80–90% of the time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1–3 months. Goal: ultimately ~2,000 most important kanji and 6–7,000 vocabulary words. Weekly target: 20–30 kanji and ~100 vocabulary words that use those kanji. Use the Radicals Mnemonic Method and/or WaniKani; narrow down meanings/readings to the most important ones first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to Read Katakana
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to read all katakana characters before unlocking much vocabulary in your kanji system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 2 days to 2 weeks. Katakana can be harder initially and appears less often early on, so prioritize hiragana and kanji first but reach basic katakana reading competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to Type Katakana
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply hiragana typing knowledge to learn katakana typing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1–2 hours. Prerequisites: able to type hiragana and read katakana. Jump to katakana section of typing guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to Type Kanji
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn how to input kanji via IME once you can read a handful (20–30) of kanji.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1–2 hours. Prerequisite: able to read 20–30 kanji. Includes tips for punctuation and symbols. Typing kanji follows similar rules to kana typing but has extra considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal Thresholds for 'Beginner' Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach concrete knowledge thresholds before focusing fully on grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target: WaniKani level 10 or roughly 300 kanji and ~1,000 vocabulary words (or equivalent using your own method) before serious grammar study. If using a resource that only teaches meaning (not reading), that does not count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a Spaced Repetition System (SRS) for Vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an SRS system to retain vocabulary learned from kanji study and from real-world encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 2–4 hours + ongoing. Have a system to record, process, and study words; don't just record words once and never review. Use dedicated SRS tools for non-kanji vocabulary; continue doing WaniKani reviews if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting Vocabulary (habit & system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect new vocabulary items consistently and in an easily accessible place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a trigger: 'if I see a word I want to learn, then I add it to my list.' Tools can be spreadsheet, Evernote, OneNote, Airtable, pocket notebook, or smartphone camera—whatever is easiest for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing Vocabulary Regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a habit to process collected vocabulary frequently and prepare them for SRS addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process daily, weekly, or monthly depending on volume. Habit formation generally takes 3–6 weeks. Make processing second nature so the flow into SRS is consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding Words to Your SRS
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer processed vocabulary into your chosen SRS with an effective card format/mnemonic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guides like 'Spaced Repetition and Japanese' and Keyword Mnemonic Method. Ensure the SRS cards are well-formed to aid long-term recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin Grammar with an 80% Knowledge Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach grammar learning only when you already know approximately 80% of the sentence's content from vocabulary/kanji.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy: each new thing should be a +1 incremental step. If you don't know enough vocabulary, return to kanji/vocab study or pre-study the sentence's vocabulary. Exceptions: very short sentences where 66–75% may be acceptable. This reduces context switching and lookup time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing and Using a Beginner Textbook/Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a textbook that fits your learning style and work through it from beginning to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated Time: 1–3 months to start, 2–6 months to get through most beginner textbooks depending on time commitment. Don't get stuck in preparation—start and make measurable progress. Combine textbooks if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering Japanese Language Questions / Fact Checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference multiple explanations and sources when you encounter confusing grammar or usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't trust a single source; some explanations are overly technical, others overly simplified. Use multiple resources to find the explanation that clicks. The guide links to 'How to Answer your Japanese Language Questions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative: Learning Grammar Independently
rubrics_metrics.description: If not using a textbook, plan ordering and resources carefully, using the know-80%-first philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering of topics is complex—follow the 'know 80%' rule and plan a sequence. Fact-check and cross-reference; be deliberate about measuring progress when self-teaching grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the Work / Avoid the Preparation Loop
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistently perform study work and measure progress instead of endlessly planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make measurable progress (e.g., pages completed, problems answered). Starting and doing is the hardest part—avoid getting trapped in planning and tool-gathering phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Use a Tutor (and what to use them for)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a tutor when stuck on issues you cannot resolve alone; focus tutor time on speaking, listening, and explanatory nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tutors are poor use for kanji/vocabulary drilling; instead use them for things only a native speaker/teacher can help with (pronunciation, nuance, answering complex questions). Not required to progress, but helpful if you need assistance beyond self-study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended Resources and Reference Books
rubrics_metrics.description: Use high-quality reference works for deeper understanding and targeted weakness remediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: The 'Basic' book from the Dictionary of Japanese Grammar series is a top reference. Focus on 'raising the floor'—work on your weaknesses (e.g., verbs) with targeted references to elevate overall ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and Prepare for the Intermediate Wall
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that intermediate stage is the hardest and many learners quit here; prepare mentally and methodologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize conscious incompetence is normal. Your advantage from kanji and vocabulary (built earlier) will help you pass this wall more quickly. Ensure all previous areas are solid before moving to intermediate materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Mnemonics and Radical-Based Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt mnemonic and radical-based kanji methods to learn kanji efficiently instead of rote memorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'Radicals Mnemonic Method' and use programs like WaniKani or create your own mnemonic-based routine. This allows learning many kanji quickly and with retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Time Estimates and Milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the guide's time estimates and milestone markers to pace learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hiragana 1 day–1 week; type hiragana 1–2 days; katakana 2 days–2 weeks; beginning kanji 1–3 months; reach ~300 kanji/1,000 vocab by beginner grammar stage; beginner textbook 2–6 months. Use these to plan and measure progress.
